PRESENTATIONS (30 minutes) a.
Enrollment Management update - Associate Vice President Libutti presented hisreport on enrollment for Fall, 2023 which had been made available in advance.
Henoted his data came from the Office for Institutional Research and he encouragedfaculty to visit that website for more detailed data and useful data visualizationtools.
Highlights of the report included the success the university is having atpreventing “summer melt,” a number that has been cut nearly in half.
The universityalso continues to grow its Talent Development program numbers and its percentageof “first in family” enrollees.
Also, for the first time, URI enrolled more out of statestudents than in-state students, which was not by design.
A couple of concerns formoving forward were noted.
First, there is a need for more student housing both oncampus and within the broader community.
It is especially concerning thatneighboring towns are increasingly hostile toward student rentals.
The universityhas had to reintroduce triple rooms which was not met with enthusiasm.
Promisingstudents, including graduate students, could be lost to competing universitiesbecause of housing.

Second, competing universities in other states are out-pacingURI in terms of ABM programs and in terms of regionalized tuition discounts(attending for an in-state rate).
This could harm enrollment in the future.
Third,there are concerns about the limitations of the Hope and Promise Scholarships andthe need for URI to be included in the state’s programs.
Other states are expandingsimilar programs, which stands to negatively affect Rhode Island, but moreimportantly, there is a question of equity and fairness for students who deserveaccess to all educational options.
Other topics were also discussed, like enrollmentby college, student preparedness, modality preferences, and overall well-being,along with the percent of adult learners/Finish What You Started programparticipants.
The Faculty Senate accepted the report. b.
Retired Faculty Association - Phillip G.
Clark, Chair of the Age-Friendly UniversityCommittee presented information on the initiative to create an RFA at URI.
TheCommittee has noted their work aligns with the One University Strategic Plan andthey have collected data from an interest survey to demonstrate the need.

TheCommittee has examined active RFA’s at peer institutions to develop a formalproposal for such organization here.
An Association would be expected to play a rolein advocacy (for various benefits and access in retirement) and in providingopportunities for connection, community and social contact.
The Committee isconsidering developing a Handbook for retired faculty that would provideinformation on issues of common interest and certain privileges that should beextended to retired faculty.
Currently, there seems to be a lot of uncertainty aroundwhich retired faculty members are extended Emeritus status and what ongoingprivileges extend to retirees (like IT support, parking, library use, attendance atathletic, cultural and other events, etc.).
Dr.
Clark stressed the mutual benefits of anRFA, noting retired faculty are a reservoir of experience and wisdom that couldcontinue to serve the community.
Following the presentation, there were questionsabout attaining Emeritus status and what privileges might come with thatdesignation.
The Provost’s office makes those designations based on tenure, type ofservice, and rank.

There were also questions about how retired faculty get hiredback for per course or other assignments and it was noted that the various collegesare involved in those decisions and there are union implications as well.
The FacultySenate voted to accept the report. 4

Federal regulations have specific stipulations about the use of “Incomplete” as a grade option that conflict with existing University Manual language.
This companion change to Report #2023-2024-07 provides clarification for this conflict.
Existing language: 8.53.20 Incomplete.
A student shall receive a temporary grade of “Incomplete” when course work has been passing but is not completed by the end of the semester due to documented extenuating circumstances beyond the ability of the student to predict and control, such as a serious illness or medical condition, or another compelling reason which justifies the grade.
An instructor who issues a grade of “Incomplete” may forward a written explanation to the student’s academic dean.

Assignment of the temporary grade of Incomplete is made sparingly and presumes both that the student intends and will be able to complete the coursework in the established time frame, and that the instructor intends and will be able to review the completed work in that established time frame. #15-16-30 #22-23-30 Proposed language: 8.53.20 Incomplete.

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-3
November 14, 2024 Faculty Senate Meeting
Context (from JCODL 2022-2023 final report): “Several years ago (circa 2013), URI adopted definitions of online and blended learning (Face to face [< 25% online], Blended [25-75% online], and Online [75-100% online]), with the implicit, but unstated, assumption that the online portion was asynchronous. The COVID era of remote instruction gave rise to additional approaches to remote instruction and the need to reflect all available modality options and to provide clear, comprehensible and accessible definitions and descriptions for the benefit of faculty and students.” Making their suggested changes also requires removing ‘Online’ from the ‘Methods of Instruction’
Existing Language:
* The Four Hundred Fifty-First Report of the Curricular Affairs Committee
* https://web.uri.edu/facsen-old/curricular-matters/method-of-instruction/
“Lecture: A course in which the primary method is presentation and students are expected to participate in a variety of ways, such as small-group discussions, questions and answers, writing-exercises, etc.

Laboratory: In-class applied course work, generally involving experimentation or observation, typically using special equipment (including computers and specialized software).
Recitation: Separate sections of a lecture course regularly scheduled for discussion.
Studio: In-class, supervised work with an emphasis on performance and creativity in which faculty instruct, assist, and critique.
Seminar: Course offered to a small group (usually no more than 20 students) where participants actively exchange ideas and findings based on readings or research.
Independent Study: One-on-one instruction in which the student enters into an agreement with the instructor that defines the focus of inquiry and nature of activities. Includes tutorials, directed readings, special projects.
Practicum: Structured experiences where the primary aim is to connect theory with practice. Includes clinics, internships, externships, student teaching, field experiences. May include regular class meetings.
Workshop: Similar to a seminar, with emphasis on applied rather than theoretical learning, but not offered for degree-program credit.

Online: A course that is delivered entirely online. (CAC policy includes possibility of a required organizational session, etc.)”

a. Announcements -
b. Status of Actions Forwarded to the President since the September 19 meeting:

a. Seconded motion: that the Faculty Senate consent to Committee
Appointments for 2024-2025 (per UM By-Laws, Section 3.4). The list has
been modified slightly since its original approval on 9/19. Some
assignments have changed slightly. Chairs have been chosen, and there

The report came to the Senate as a motion by FSEC. The motion was seconded and approved.

a. Update on the Division of Research and Economic Development from Vice President Bethany Jenkins. VP Jenkins offered a brief report that addressed the mission of her office, highlighted student success initiatives, and listed several recent faulty funding awards. She then presented data on research dollars secured so far this year by source and college. She then updated the Senate on staffing changes and additions. The Research and Economic Development division has prioritized providing support to principal investigators in developing proposals and managing projects. They have launched a Research Concierge model that should serve as a point of contact for PIs and grant administrators at all stages and proactively develop guidelines, policies, and operating procedures that will become long-lasting, proactive resources for faculty.

a. Joint Committee on Online and Distance Learning - Annual Report for AY 2023-2024 - Christopher Lavan, Assoc. Vice Provost for Advancement of Teaching and Learning presented the annual report, noting the tasks that the committee dedicated itself to last year along with its priorities for AY 24-25. One of the themes of AY 23-24 was addressing learning modalities and the committee agreed upon a set of defined modalities that should be advancing for Senate approval soon. AVP Lavan also sought to dispel some myths around certifications for online instructors and offered a handout that addressed online pedagogy and all the pathways currently available to faculty to become qualified online instructors.
b. Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee Reports - Chair Ward i. CBUM Report #2024-2025-1, Amendments to Appendix C of the
University Manual (Faculty Senate By-Laws), Sections 4.20 and 4.27.
1st reading -Introduction (Requested Action: Motion to continue to

ii. CBUM Informational Report - Goals and Priorities for the Year - Chair Ward reported on her committee’s top three priorities for the academic year. They include: version control of the University Manual; considering the relationship between the faculty’s CBA and the University Manual and whether or not there is a need for direct links to the contract within the Manual; and assisting with the reimagining of the Honors Program. i. Report #2024-2025-1A, Courses - Several course changes in CELS, CHS, A&S and COB were noted. In terms of new courses, several were proposed across six colleges. iii. Report #2024-2025 -1C, New Programs - The report addressed one new program in the College of Education, which was approved.
d. Curriculum and Standards Committee - Chair Trimm
i. Report 2024-2025-02 on Proposed Amendments to Section 8.22.40 of the University Manual, Academic Regulations; “Distinction.”

(Requested Action: Motion to approve the report) - The report called for a language change in Chapter 8 that would provide much-needed clarity around the minimum number of graded credits required to graduate with distinction. Examples of students affected by the current lack of clarity were offered during discussion, and several questions were asked about the proposal’s allowance of up to 5 credits of S/U coursework. There was agreement that this was a reasonable number that could certainly be modified in the future, if necessary. The proposal was approved unanimously.
ii. Report No. 2024-2025-1A, Courses
(Requested Action: Motion to approve the report) - Chair Trimm addressed the report which contained one informational matter and eight course changes requiring approval. One of the eight items listed was withdrawn by the Department (Math 101). The report was approved.
iii. Report No. 2024-2025-1B, Programs
(Requested Action: Motion to approve the report) - The report addressed two program modifications (Landscape Architecture and Interdisciplinary Neuroscience). Both were approved.
iv. SSCC Report No. 2024-2025-03C, New Program

(Requested Action: Motion to approve the report) - Chair Trimm presented the report covering one new program (BA Business Studies) and the report was approved.
e. General Education Committee - Chair Fogelman
i. Report No. 2024-2025-02 (Requested Action: Motion to approve the report) - The brief report covering one course change and two new courses was approved.

9. OPEN FACULTY FORUM: Textbooks and other Course Materials’ availability from the University Bookstore and Library - Faculty Senate Vice President Williams provided some background information on the issue, noting that faculty have an ethical obligation as well as a legal one to use the university bookstore as a clearinghouse for course materials. Because buy-backs and rental options have all but disappeared, early adoption of textbooks is crucial if the bookstore is to be able to provide them in a timely fashion. The growth in use of apps and other alternatives poses special challenges for certain groups of students, especially international and talent development students and those relying on Federal Financial Aid. Useful suggestions pertained to providing information to students during orientation regarding course materials and involving department heads and deans in course material decisions to help ensure an equitable approach. A representative of the Campus Bookstore, Manager Paul Whitney, was on hand to offer their perspective. He noted that publishers’ “editioning” and the rise of Amazon are two of the biggest changes the industry has seen in the last couple of decades. Some faculty members complained that there seems to be excess bureaucracy involved in dealing with the campus bookstore in that, even if the course is not requiring materials through the bookstore, their forms still need to be completed every year. It was suggested that there may be a technical fix to help reduce that burden.

10. OLD BUSINESS: (10 minutes)
a. Centers and Institutes - Update from President Walls - Pres. Walls noted that a meeting schedule throughout the Fall has been set with the Provost’s office to develop a new model for creating and renewing Centers and Institutes. The goal is to have a proposal for the Senate at the December meeting.
b. Eldercare Issues affecting faculty - Update from President Walls - There are plans to circle back to this issue at the November meeting.
11. CALL for NEW BUSINESS - None.
12. ADJOURNMENT - The meeting adjourned at 4:54 PM.

Joint Curriculum & Standards Committee and Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report #2024-2025-01
The following matter was discussed and recommended by the Curriculum & Standards Committee at their October 31, 2024 meeting, and later supported by the Faculty Senate Executive Committee. It is now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval.
Context: Currently, courses approved for online formats during the traditional academic calendar (Fall/Spring 14-weeks, J-Term, and Summer 5- and 10-weeks) must complete a full curricular review to be added to the URI Online Accelerated calendar (7-week Fall, Spring, and Summer sessions).
Proposed: Any course approved for online instruction is thereby approved for being offered in all online semester calendars: 14-week, J-Term, Summer (5 and 10 week), and accelerated 7-week terms.

V. 23.09.29 CURRICULUM & STANDARDS COMMITTEE FACULTY SENATE OFFICE URI Curriculum & Standards Committee Non-Standard form for curricular changes Only to be used in cases not appropriate for Kuali A Proposal to Fully Integrate the Public Relations Program into the Department of Journalism, Creating a New Department of Journalism and Public Relations Date: 10/27/23 Proposer Name: Professor Norbert Mundorf Department: Communication Studies 1.
Describe the change you are proposing.
This organization change will bring the Public Relations B.A. program, which is currently housed in the Communication Studies department, and the Journalism B.A. program together in a new Journalism and Public Relations department. 2.
Give the rationale for your proposed change.
In 1997, the B.A. in Public Relations was approved as an interdepartmental program jointly run by the Communication Studies department and the Journalism department.

The original legislation (Bill #96- 97-26) called for the program to be administered on a “three-year rotating basis by the Chairs of Journalism and Communication Studies” with an “advisory/admissions committee” comprised of both chairs from the respective departments and the faculty who taught in the program.
Somewhere in the twenty-five plus years that have elapsed since the original proposal, the Public Relations program was effectively subsumed by Communication Studies and the interdepartmental structure of the original vision was lost.
During the academic program review of Journalism this past year, external reviewers suggested the Journalism curriculum would benefit from a “rethinking of [Harrington’s] overall department structure.” While it was originally proposed that the department might merge with the program in Sports Media Communication, subsequent conversations with faculty suggested that public relations would be a better fit as this pairing is common in institutions across the country and presents additional opportunities for collaboration due to the curricular overlap between the two programs.
Interestingly, the original proposal to create the public relations program also emphasized the importance of this relationship: “Because the existing Public Relations courses are Journalism courses,

V. 23.09.29 because the existing minor has been administered by the chair of Journalism, and because of the extent of the chair’s involvement in the existing internship program, the chair of Journalism will serve as the initial administrator of the program.” Following the guidance of the reviewers and in the spirit of the original vision for this program, the proposed organizational change will restore the interdisciplinary vision for the Public Relations program. It will allow for resource sharing and interdisciplinary collaboration between programs and will also help to rectify a primary issue addressed in the Journalism academic program review, namely, the absence of a Chair. In order to address this leadership gap and ensure a successful start to this new department, a search for a Full Professor who will Chair this new department is currently underway. 3. This change will affect the Public Relations BA program (currently housed in Communication Studies department) and Journalism BA program and Journalism department. These units are housed in the Harrington School of Communication and Media in the College of Arts and Sciences. 4. Include any necessary letters of support. The University of Rhode Island is an equal opportunity employer committed to community, equity, and diversity and to the principles of affirmative action. 29 October 2023 Support for new Department of Journalism and Public Relations As Dean of Arts and Sciences, I fully support the proposed integration of Public Relations with the Journalism Department to create a new Department of Journalism and Public Relations. This merger does not impact the academic programs in any way. Nationally, many institutions have journalism and public relations programs in the same department. Students and faculty both benefit from the synergies between the two disciplines. The merger will also enable more effective use of resources, while also freeing the Department of Communication Studies to focus more fully on their major, as well as continue to provide a home for the rapidly expanding sports communication and media major. The Journalism and Public Relations faculty have all discussed and confirmed their agreement to merge. A full professor line has been allocated for this initiative, and the individual hired will serve as chair; a search committee composed of faculty from both majors has been established. Further, I am committed to providing faculty lines to move fully resource both majors given their import and student interest.
